Privacy Auditing with Zero (0) Training Run

Tudor Cebere ††thanks: Equal contribution Affiliation: PreMeDICaL team, Inria Affiliation: Idesp, Inserm, Univ. de Montpellier    Mathieu Even11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: PreMeDICaL team, Inria Affiliation: Idesp, Inserm, Univ. de Montpellier    Linus Bleistein Affiliation: School of Computer and Communication Affiliation: Sciences and School of Life Sciences (EPFL)    Aurélien Bellet Affiliation: PreMeDICaL team, Inria Affiliation: Idesp, Inserm, Univ. de Montpellier
Abstract

Privacy auditing provides empirical lower bounds on the differential privacy parameters of learning algorithms. Existing methods, however, require interventional access to the training pipeline, either to retrain multiple times or to randomize data inclusion. This is often infeasible for large deployed systems such as foundation models. We introduce Zero-Run privacy auditing, a post-hoc framework for auditing models using two fixed datasets: examples known to be training-set members and examples known to be non-members. In this observational regime, membership is no longer randomized; instead, member and non-member data often differ in distribution, so membership inference scores may reflect a distribution shift rather than algorithmic leakage. Drawing on ideas from causal inference, we formalize this confounding effect and propose two complementary corrections that yield valid privacy audits. Our first approach models the combined effect of distribution shift and algorithmic leakage as an adaptive composition, producing conservative global corrections. Our second approach conditions on observed data and adjusts pointwise membership guesses, yielding sharper instance-dependent bounds. Experiments on synthetic data and large-scale models show that Zero-Run auditing enables practical privacy evaluation when retraining or controlled data insertion is infeasible.

1 Introduction

As AI systems increasingly process sensitive data, mitigating privacy leakage (i.e., the inadvertent disclosure of training examples) has become a critical priority. This risk is exacerbated by high-capacity foundation models trained across various modalities [39, 21, 32, 7, 18, 8]. Trained on massive, web-crawled corpora, they are inherently susceptible to memorizing personal or proprietary information [4, 3, 24], and Carlini et al. [2] show that this memorization scales log-linearly with model size. Moreover, these vulnerabilities introduce challenges in domain-specific contexts; for instance, clinical foundation models memorize rare patient profiles despite rigorous data de-identification [38].

A countermeasure to these risks is differential privacy (DP) [12], the de facto standard for privacy-preserving algorithms. By bounding the impact of any individual’s data on the result, DP protects against privacy attacks that infer sensitive information from released outputs. However, despite offering worst-case guarantees over the privacy leakage, its adoption in large-scale training pipelines is limited due to steep utility penalties [20] and the prohibitive cost of overhauling existing data-processing infrastructure [35].

Motivated by these practical barriers, privacy auditing offers an empirical complement to DP by lower-bounding an algorithm’s privacy parameters [9, 19, 29, 5]. By probing a model’s behavior on its training data, audits can expose implementation flaws [40], identify misconfigured privacy mechanisms [6], or demonstrate that theoretical guarantees are tight (i.e., the auditing lower bound closely matches the DP upper bound) [30, 29]. In contrast to worst-case theoretical upper bounds, auditing quantifies empirical leakage for a specific model architecture, dataset, and threat model, yielding deployment-relevant evidence for privacy claims, compliance, and risk assessment [15].

While traditional privacy auditing requires repeatedly retraining models on randomized datasets [19, 29, 5], recent advances condense this requirement to a single randomized training run [37, 25]. Yet, even this approach fails to scale to modern AI models. Their training consumes thousands of GPU days and relies on rigid, distributed data pipelines. Large language models perfectly capture this dilemma. Despite being trained on vast web corpora loaded with sensitive data, their immense scale, opaque data mixtures, and blackbox deployments render privacy auditing nearly impossible. Consequently, researchers and regulators lack tools to verify privacy guarantees, relying on trust and the voluntary cooperation of model providers. This creates an accountability gap: the systems posing the greatest privacy risks are the most insulated from independent privacy evaluation.

Contributions. To address this gap, we introduce a Zero-Run auditing framework that enables auditors to assess the privacy leakage of an algorithm post-hoc from its release, without modifying the algorithm or data pipeline. We ground our approach in a fundamental analogy to causal inference. Existing privacy audits based on randomized data insertion are inherently interventional—analogous to randomized controlled trials—which avoid confounding by design. In contrast, our Zero-Run framework is the observational counterpart, estimating privacy leakage from static member and non-member datasets. Since these datasets often follow different underlying distributions, this distribution shift acts as a confounding factor [33, 42]. Guided by this analogy, our main contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    Formalizing Zero-Run Auditing (Section 3). We formalize the post-hoc auditing regime where the auditor relies on disjoint datasets of known members and non-members. We demonstrate that naive audits on such data can substantially overestimate privacy leakage: membership inference attacks can succeed merely by exploiting distributional shift rather than algorithmic leakage, causing standard procedures to wrongly attribute this spurious signal to the model. We explicitly connect this setting to observational causal inference, where valid correction requires overlap (positivity) between the member and non-member distributions.

  2. 2.

    Privacy Leakage Correction (Sections 4 and 5). We extend One-Run analyses [37, 25] to the post-hoc regime, correcting distribution shift effects on empirical privacy curves via:

    • •

      The Composition Viewpoint (Section 4) models the observed leakage as an adaptive composition of a distribution-shift mechanism and the audited algorithm, yielding a deconvolution-based estimate of privacy leakage, albeit a conservative one under severe distribution shift.

    • •

      The Conditional Viewpoint (Section 5) characterizes pointwise privacy leakage conditional on the example. We tamper an adversary’s membership guesses to remove overconfidence induced by confounding, yielding a robust, shift-dependent correction.

  3. 3.

    Propensity Scores and Uncertainty Quantification (Section 6). Our composition and conditional correction principles rely on propensity scores (the probability that an example is a member, based solely on its features), which must be estimated. We explicitly quantify uncertainty in propensity score estimation in our privacy lower bounds via bootstrapping [14].

  4. 4.

    Practical Scalability (Section 7). We demonstrate that Zero-Run auditing enables scalable privacy audits of large, deployed models where retraining is computationally or logistically infeasible.

2 Background on Differential Privacy and Privacy Auditing

Differential Privacy. Informally, Differential Privacy (DP) [12, 13] ensures that a randomized algorithm’s output remains largely unchanged whether a single individual’s data is included or not in the input. DP is widely considered the standard for privacy-preserving data analysis because it provides a mathematically rigorous guarantee against adversaries with arbitrary side information. DP is immune to post-processing (protections cannot be degraded by further computation) and composes gracefully, enabling accurate tracking of the cumulative privacy loss across multiple analyses.

Definition 1 ((ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP).

Let ε,δ>0\varepsilon,\delta>0. A randomized algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that takes as input a dataset 𝒟⊂𝒳\mathcal{D}\subset\mathcal{X} and outputs 𝒜⁡(𝒟)∈Θ\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D})\in\Theta is said to satisfy (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-differential privacy if, for any pair of adjacent datasets 𝒟\mathcal{D} and 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} (i.e., which are the same except one data sample) and any measurable set ℰ⊂Θ\mathcal{E}\subset\Theta:

ℙ⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒟)∈ℰ)≤eε​ℙ​(𝒜⁡(𝒟′)∈ℰ)+δ.\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D})\in\mathcal{E}\right)\leq e^{\varepsilon}\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}^{\prime})\in\mathcal{E}\right)+\delta\,.

Pure ε\varepsilon-DP corresponds to the special case where δ=0\delta=0. In this work, we will also rely on the more expressive notion of ff-DP [10], which is based on trade-off functions that lower bound the Type II error given a Type I error of α\alpha for testing z∼ℙz\sim\mathbb{P} versus z∼ℚz\sim\mathbb{Q}. We denote by TZ,Z′T_{Z,Z^{\prime}} the trade-off function between the distributions of two random variables Z,Z′Z,Z^{\prime}.

Definition 2 (Trade-off function).

For two distributions ℙ\mathbb{P} and ℚ\mathbb{Q} on some space 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, the trade-off function Tℙ,ℚT_{\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q}} is the function [0,1]→[0,1][0,1]\to[0,1] defined as Tℙ,ℚ​(α)=inf{βϕ|αϕ≤α}T_{\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=\inf{\left\{\beta_{\phi}\,|\,\alpha_{\phi}\leq\alpha\right\}}, where the infimum is taken over all measurable functions 𝒵→{0,1}\mathcal{Z}\to{\left\{0,1\right\}}, αϕ=𝔼ℙ​ϕ\alpha_{\phi}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\phi and βϕ=𝔼ℚ​ϕ\beta_{\phi}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}\phi.

Definition 3 (ff-DP).

A randomized algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} is said to satisfy ff-differential privacy for ff a decreasing and convex function satisfying f⁡(t)≤1−tf(t)\leq 1-t for t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] if, for any pair of adjacent datasets 𝒟\mathcal{D} and 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime}, we have, for all α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], T𝒜⁡(𝒟),𝒜⁡(𝒟′)​(α)≥f⁡(α)T_{\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}),\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}^{\prime})}(\alpha)\geq f(\alpha). Equivalently, for any measurable set ℰ\mathcal{E}, ℙ⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒟)∈ℰ)≤f¯​(ℙ⁡(𝒜⁡(𝒟′)∈ℰ))\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D})\in\mathcal{E}\right)\leq\bar{f}\big(\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}^{\prime})\in\mathcal{E}\right)\big), where f¯=1−f.\bar{f}=1-f.

For two mechanisms 𝒜1\mathcal{A}_{1} and 𝒜2\mathcal{A}_{2}, respectively f1f_{1}-DP and f2f_{2}-DP, their composition 𝒜2⊙𝒜1\mathcal{A}_{2}\odot\mathcal{A}_{1} satisfies ff-DP, with ff given by the convolution f=f1⊗f2f=f_{1}\otimes f_{2}, which characterizes the optimal testing error after observing both outputs. This remains valid even if 𝒜2\mathcal{A}_{2} depends on the outputs of 𝒜1\mathcal{A}_{1} [10]. Two special cases of ff-DP will be used throughout: (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP (Definition 1), summarized by parameters (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta), and Gaussian DP (μ\mu-GDP, [10]), summarized by a scalar μ\mu, with respective trade-off functions fε,δ​(p)=max⁡(0,1−eε​p−δ,e−ε​(1−δ−p))f_{\varepsilon,\delta}(p)=\max(0,1-e^{\varepsilon}p-\delta,e^{-\varepsilon}(1-\delta-p)) and OPENGμ​(p)=Φ⁡(Φ−1​(1−p)−μ))G_{\mu}(p)=\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1-p)-\mu)). For μ\mu-GDP, the function ff coincides with the false negative rate as a function of the false positive rate for the optimal test distinguishing two unit-variance Gaussians with means differing by μ\mu. While (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP summarizes privacy using two worst-case parameters, ff-DP and GDP characterize the full trade-off between false positives and false negatives. This finer description provides a complete view of an adversary’s inference capability and enables more expressive privacy reporting and accounting [17].

Privacy Auditing. An auditing algorithm takes as input an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} (e.g., DP-SGD) and a privacy hypothesis ℋ\mathcal{H} (e.g., “𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfies ff-DP”), outputting a bit indicating whether 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfies ℋ\mathcal{H}. Standard auditing follows a three-step procedure: (1) a randomized experiment evaluating 𝒜\mathcal{A} on a dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}; (2) a membership inference attack (MIA) outputting guesses (Ti)i∈[m]∈{−1,0,1}m(T_{i})_{i\in[m]}\in{\left\{-1,0,1\right\}}^{m} for the true membership SiS_{i} of XiX_{i} based on the output of the experiment, with Ti=0T_{i}=0 denoting abstention; and (3) an audit evaluation outputting b∈{True,False}b\in{\left\{\textsc{True},\textsc{False}\right\}} based on ℋ\mathcal{H}, the MIA output TT, and the experiment’s observations (including true memberships). For an error probability p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1], the audit is pp-valid if ℙ⁡(b=False|𝒜​ satisfies ​ℋ)≤p\mathbb{P}\left(b=\textsc{False}|\mathcal{A}\text{ satisfies }\mathcal{H}\right)\leq p. From such procedures, one can derive empirical privacy parameters—high-probability lower bounds on leakage—by identifying the largest privacy level confidently ruled out by the audit (see Section 6).

In step (1), both Multi-Run [19] and One-Run [37] auditing randomize data inclusions—executing 𝒜\mathcal{A} repeatedly for individual points XiX_{i}, or once for multiple points (Xi)i∈[m](X_{i})_{i\in[m]}, respectively. Both rely fundamentally on membership indicators Si∈{−1,1}S_{i}\in\{-1,1\} being independent, centered random variables. This randomized assignment is the core statistical assumption validating interventional audits, an assumption that our Zero-Run auditing framework explicitly eliminates.

3 Zero-Run Privacy Auditing Framework

Traditional privacy auditing techniques rely on randomized experiments (see Section 2) that demand computationally prohibitive re-executions and randomized data insertions, making them infeasible for complex, large-scale systems. We address this bottleneck by replacing the interventional experiment with an observational study. Instead of randomizing input data and re-running the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A}, our Zero-Run auditor passively evaluates its existing output. This approach requires zero control over or access to the original execution pipeline.

Zero-Run Auditing. As illustrated in Figure 1, our Zero-Run auditing framework operates as follows:

  1. 1.

    (Algorithm Output & Observational Data Formulation) The auditor observes θ=𝒜⁡(𝒟train)\theta=\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}), the result of the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} executed on a private dataset 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}. This output might be accessible via direct inspection or indirectly through a query interface. Crucially, the auditor lacks access to the full dataset 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} and the algorithm’s internal mechanics. Instead, the auditor relies on observational data: known members 𝒟1⊂𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{1}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} and known non-members 𝒟0⊂𝒳∖𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{0}\subset\mathcal{X}\setminus\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}. Let {X1,…,Xm}=𝒟1∪𝒟0{\left\{X_{1},\ldots,X_{m}\right\}}=\mathcal{D}_{1}\cup\mathcal{D}_{0} represent the combined data, with true membership indicators defined by Si=1S_{i}=1 if Xi∈𝒟1X_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{1} and Si=−1S_{i}=-1 if Xi∈𝒟0X_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{0}. Unlike traditional randomized experiments, the membership variables Si∈{−1,1}S_{i}\in{\left\{-1,1\right\}} are not centered; rather, SiS_{i} inherently depends on the data features XiX_{i}, as 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} and 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} may exhibit a distribution shift.

  2. 2.

    (Membership Inference) Leveraging the accessible algorithm output θ\theta and the features XiX_{i} from the observational data, the auditor runs a Membership Inference Attack (MIA). This step produces raw membership guesses TiT_{i} for each XiX_{i}. Formally, the MIA is a mapping (θ,(Xi)i∈[m])↦T∈{−1,0,1}m(\theta,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]})\mapsto T\in{\left\{-1,0,1\right\}}^{m}, where a guess of Ti=1T_{i}=1 indicates membership, Ti=−1T_{i}=-1 indicates non-membership, and Ti=0T_{i}=0 corresponds to abstention (e.g., low confidence). Further details on the MIA meta-algorithm are provided in Algorithm 5 (Section B.3).

  3. 3.

    (Propensity Estimator) To mitigate bias in raw MIA estimates caused by distribution shifts between members and non-members, we calculate an estimated propensity score, π^​(Xi)\hat{\pi}(X_{i}). This approximates the true propensity π:𝒳→[0,1]\pi:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1], defined formally as π⁡(x)=ℙ⁡(Si=1∣Xi=x)\pi(x)=\mathbb{P}(S_{i}=1\mid X_{i}=x). By capturing the inherent probability that a data point belongs to the training set based solely on its features, this score isolates structural selection likelihood from the signal contained in the algorithm’s output. Section 6 details this estimation and its induced uncertainty propagation.

  4. 4.

    (Zero-Run Correction) Finally, the framework combines the true labels SiS_{i}, the raw MIA guesses TiT_{i}, and the propensity scores π^​(Xi)\hat{\pi}(X_{i}) to produce a statistically valid audit evaluation. This correction stage effectively disentangles the algorithm’s actual privacy leakage from the underlying data distribution shift, and stems from our main theoretical contributions (Sections 4 and 5). The correction can be applied compositionally (yielding global bounds) or conditionally (yielding pointwise bounds), outputting empirical DP lower bounds.

This four-step meta-algorithm forms the backbone of our Zero-Run auditing framework. To ensure a provably valid audit, a specific assumption for the generation of datasets 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} and 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} is required.

Assumption 1 (Data Generation).

Datasets 𝒟1={Xi:Si=1}\mathcal{D}_{1}={\left\{X_{i}:S_{i}=1\right\}} and 𝒟0={Xi:Si=−1}\mathcal{D}_{0}={\left\{X_{i}:S_{i}=-1\right\}}, representing members and non-members respectively, consist of independent samples drawn from distributions ℙ1\mathbb{P}_{1} and ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{0}, of identical sizes n1=n0n_{1}=n_{0}.

There are several strategies for sourcing members and non-members, depending on the use case.

Member dataset 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1}. This dataset can be any subset of the training set of the audited model, such as a random subsample or a curated subset selected to maximize potential privacy leakage. Even when the complete primary dataset is unknown to the auditor, it is often possible to identify some included examples. For instance, when auditing large-scale models, 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} may consist of public records, historical archives, or corpora published prior to the algorithm’s execution phase [34, 27, 28].

Non-member dataset 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0}. The most straightforward scenario occurs when a randomized test split is available, yielding a dataset 𝒟0⊂𝒳∖𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{0}\subset\mathcal{X}\setminus\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} with zero distribution shift. When such a split is unavailable, alternative construction strategies are necessary. Following empirical evaluations for large language models [28], one approach is to utilize data generated after the algorithm’s execution timestamp, ensuring 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} is strictly excluded; however, a distribution shift (ℙ1≠ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{1}\neq\mathbb{P}_{0}) is naturally expected here due to temporal changes. Alternatively, one can synthesize non-members from a continuous approximation of the member distribution by training a generative model on 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} and sampling from it, yielding non-members with a close distributional match (ℙ0≈ℙ1\mathbb{P}_{0}\approx\mathbb{P}_{1}), as seen in Panoramia [23]. Our framework seamlessly integrates these varied choices of 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0}.

Remark 1.

We emphasize that, as in [37, 25], our meta-algorithm does not restrict the auditor to algorithms that formally satisfy DP. Because our framework treats 𝒜\mathcal{A} as a black box and evaluates privacy leakage purely based on its outputs and observational data, it can be applied to arbitrary algorithms, regardless of whether they were designed with formal privacy guarantees.

4 A Global Correction via Adaptive Composition

If ℙ1=ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{1}=\mathbb{P}_{0}, membership is independent of the features XiX_{i}, so One-Run audits apply directly: the observed member/non-member labels behave like randomized inclusion bits. Under distribution shift (ℙ1≠ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{1}\neq\mathbb{P}_{0}), however, the features themselves carry information about the membership bits SiS_{i}. An auditor may therefore appear to perform well by exploiting distribution-shift signals rather than privacy leakage from the algorithm’s output.

Distribution Shift as Adaptive Composition. We account for this baseline distribution-shift leakage by modeling the auditor’s observations—the audit dataset (Xi)i∈[m](X_{i})_{i\in[m]} and the output θ=𝒜⁡(𝒟train)\theta=\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}})—as the composition of two randomized mechanisms: a distribution-shift mechanism ℳDS\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{DS}}, which generates the audit data (Xi)i∈[m](X_{i})_{i\in[m]} from the membership bits, and the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A}, which outputs θ=𝒜⁡(𝒟train)\theta=\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}). This composition view lets us use DP composition to separate spurious leakage due to distribution shift from the algorithm’s actual privacy leakage.

Formally, let ℳTot\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Tot}} be a virtual global randomized mechanism acting on a private membership vector s∈{−1,1}ms\in{\left\{-1,1\right\}}^{m}. The auditor’s available observations are thus the output of two composed mechanisms applied to the hidden bits: ℳTot​(s)=(ℳDS​(s),ℳ𝒜​(ℳDS​(s),s))\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Tot}}(s)=\big(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{DS}}(s),\,\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{DS}}(s),s)\big), where :

ℳDS(s)∼∏i=1m(𝟙{si=1}𝒫1+𝟙{si=−1}𝒫0),ℳ𝒜(x,s)=𝒜(𝒟∪{xi:si=1}),\textstyle\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{DS}}(s)\sim\prod_{i=1}^{m}\big(\mathds{1}_{\left\{s_{i}=1\right\}}\mathcal{P}_{1}+\mathds{1}_{\left\{s_{i}=-1\right\}}\mathcal{P}_{0}\big),\quad\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}(x,s)=\mathcal{A}\big(\mathcal{D}\cup{\left\{x_{i}:s_{i}=1\right\}}\big)\,,

with 𝒟=𝒟train∖𝒟1\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}\setminus\mathcal{D}_{1}. ℳDS\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{DS}} samples the audit examples from the member or non-member distribution according to their membership bits, and ℳ𝒜\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}} runs the algorithm on the examples whose bits indicate membership, such that the following holds.

Theorem 4.1.

Under Assumption 1 and if 𝒜\mathcal{A} is ff-DP, ℳDS\mathcal{M}_{{\mathrm{DS}}} is fDSf_{{\mathrm{DS}}}-DP, then ℳTot\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Tot}} is fTotf_{{\mathrm{Tot}}}-DP with fTot=f⊗fDS,f_{{\mathrm{Tot}}}=f\otimes f_{{\mathrm{DS}}}\,, where ⊗\otimes is the tensor product between trade-off functions [10, Section 3].

Remark 2.

In Theorem 4.1, 𝒜\mathcal{A} takes as input elements of 𝒳\mathcal{X} (data points), and DP for 𝒜\mathcal{A} is defined using the Add/Remove definition of adjacency. ℳTot\mathcal{M}_{{\mathrm{Tot}}} and ℳDS\mathcal{M}_{{\mathrm{DS}}} take as inputs elements of {−1,1}{\left\{-1,1\right\}} (bits): DP for these two mechanisms is thus defined using the Replace definition of adjacency. Replace for membership bits is equivalent to Add/Remove for data points.

Theorem 4.1 accounts for distribution shift in the observed privacy leakage by formalizing how leakage from the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} combines with that of the audit data. However, the fDSf_{{\mathrm{DS}}}-DP guarantee becomes vacuous if severe distribution shift causes the raw features XiX_{i} to completely leak membership information, driving the underlying trade-off function Tℙ0,ℙ1T_{\mathbb{P}_{0},\mathbb{P}_{1}} to zero, effectively shadowing out the algorithmic leakage of 𝒜\mathcal{A} and yielding uninformative lower bounds. Consequently, we require the likelihood ratio between ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{0} and ℙ1\mathbb{P}_{1} to be bounded almost surely, which motivates our next assumption. Recall that π⁡(x)=ℙ⁡(Si=1∣Xi=x)\pi(x)=\mathbb{P}(S_{i}=1\mid X_{i}=x) denotes the propensity score function.

Assumption 2 (Approximate overlap).

There exists η∈(0,1/2)\eta\in(0,1/2) and δDS∈(0,1)\delta_{\mathrm{DS}}\in(0,1) such that ℙ1​(π⁡(Xi)∈[η,1−η])≥1−δDS\mathbb{P}_{1}(\pi(X_{i})\in[\eta,1-\eta])\geq 1-\delta_{\mathrm{DS}} and ℙ0​(π⁡(Xi)∈[η,1−η])≥1−δDS\mathbb{P}_{0}(\pi(X_{i})\in[\eta,1-\eta])\geq 1-\delta_{\mathrm{DS}}.

Under overlap, upper-bounding the ℳDS\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{DS}} trade-off function enables standard One-Run auditing on ℳTot\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Tot}}. Excess leakage beyond ℳDS\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{DS}} is then attributed to 𝒜\mathcal{A} to provide valid empirical lower bounds.

Corollary 1.

Under 1 and 2, let ε,δ,μ>0\varepsilon,\delta,\mu>0, ε¯DS=log⁡(1−ηη)\bar{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{DS}}=\log(\frac{1-\eta}{\eta}), and μ¯DS=Φ−1​(eε¯DS1+eε¯DS)−Φ−1​(11+eε¯DS)\bar{\mu}_{\mathrm{DS}}=\Phi^{-1}(\frac{e^{\bar{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{DS}}}}{1+e^{\bar{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{DS}}}})-\Phi^{-1}(\frac{1}{1+e^{\bar{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{DS}}}}). Then, (1) if ℳTot\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Tot}} is not (ε+ε¯DS,1−(1−δ)​(1−δDS))(\varepsilon+\bar{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{DS}},1-(1-\delta)(1-\delta_{\mathrm{DS}}))-DP, then 𝒜\mathcal{A} is not (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP; (2) if ℳTot\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Tot}} is not Gμ2+μ¯DS2⊗f0,δDSG_{\sqrt{\mu^{2}+\bar{\mu}_{\mathrm{DS}}^{2}}}\otimes f_{0,\delta_{\mathrm{DS}}}-DP, then 𝒜\mathcal{A} is not μ\mu-GDP.

According to the above compositional view, a valid Zero-Run audit (which rejects with probability 1−p′1-p^{\prime}) of hypothesis ℋ\mathcal{H} on 𝒜\mathcal{A} can thus be obtained by interpreting it as applying a One-Run audit (which rejects with probability 1−p1-p) to mechanism ℳTot\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Tot}} using a deflated hypothesis ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime}. Corollary 1 yields two practical instances of this reduction argument. If ℳTot\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Tot}} violates the deflated hypothesis ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} below, then 𝒜\mathcal{A} violates the target hypothesis ℋ\mathcal{H}: (1) for (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP Auditing: ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} is “ℳTot\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Tot}} is (ε+ε¯DS,1−(1−δ)​(1−δDS))(\varepsilon+\bar{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{DS}},1-(1-\delta)(1-\delta_{\mathrm{DS}}))-DP” and p′=pp^{\prime}=p [37]; and (2) for μ\mu-GDP Auditing: ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} is “ℳTot\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Tot}} is (μ+μDS)(\mu+\mu_{\mathrm{DS}})-GDP” and p′=p+δDSp^{\prime}=p+\delta_{\mathrm{DS}} [25]. The resulting audit algorithms (Sections B.4 and B.5) are however conservative, as they assign worst-case distribution-shift leakage uniformly across all data points, even when propensity scores are highly heterogeneous. We address this by conditioning on the observed examples and adjusting each membership guess using its corresponding propensity score.

5 A Pointwise Correction via Conditional Auditing

Modeling distribution shift globally via ℳDS\mathcal{M}_{{\mathrm{DS}}} imposes a pessimistic, worst-case DP leakage, ε¯DS=supx∈𝒳εDS​(x)\bar{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{DS}}=\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DS}}(x) where εDS​(x)=|log⁡π⁡(x)−log⁡(1−π⁡(x))|\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DS}}(x)=\left|\log\pi(x)-\log\left(1-\pi(x)\right)\right| . This supremum reduces the audit’s statistical power, as the local leakage εDS​(Xi)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DS}}(X_{i}) for most observed data points (Xi)i∈[m](X_{i})_{i\in[m]} is typically much smaller than ε¯DS\bar{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{DS}}. To overcome this penalty, we leverage pointwise leakage. Conditioned on an observation Xi=xiX_{i}=x_{i}, the distribution shift’s contribution to inferring SiS_{i} reduces to the exact local log-odds εDS​(xi)\varepsilon_{{\mathrm{DS}}}(x_{i}). For an ε\varepsilon-DP algorithm, the combined evidence increases the correct membership odds by at most ε+εDS​(xi)\varepsilon+\varepsilon_{{\mathrm{DS}}}(x_{i}), upper-bounding the probability of a successful guess (Ti=SiT_{i}=S_{i}) by:

pi​(ε)=eε+εDS​(Xi)1+eε+εDS​(Xi).\textstyle p_{i}(\varepsilon)=\frac{e^{\varepsilon+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DS}}(X_{i})}}{1+e^{\varepsilon+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DS}}(X_{i})}}\,.

Tampered Membership Guess. To leverage pointwise leakage, our conditional audit bounds the success rate of an independently tampered MIA. Intuitively, tampering acts as randomized abstention: if an example has a highly imbalanced propensity score, a correct guess is less indicative of algorithmic leakage because it could easily be inferred from XiX_{i} alone. We therefore retain such guesses with lower probability, while keeping guesses for examples with π⁡(Xi)\pi(X_{i}) closer to 1/21/2.

Formally, given initial MIA predictions (Ti)i∈[m]∈{−1,0,1}m(T_{i})_{i\in[m]}\in{\left\{-1,0,1\right\}}^{m}, we define the post-processed tampered predictions as Ti′=Bi​TiT_{i}^{\prime}=B_{i}T_{i}, where (Bi)i∈[m]∈{0,1}m(B_{i})_{i\in[m]}\in{\left\{0,1\right\}}^{m} are independent Bernoulli variables with parameter bib_{i} conditioned on XX. Because our probabilistic bounds depend on the observed features (Xi)i∈[m](X_{i})_{i\in[m]}, this approach yields a conditional audit rather than a global worst-case one. As the following theorem demonstrates, this conditional tampering ensures that the number of correct retained guesses is stochastically controlled by the standard benchmark for One-Run auditing without distribution shift, allowing us to pay only pointwise propensity penalties.

Theorem 5.1 (Conditional Auditing).

Assume Assumption 1 holds and the attacker makes at most r∈[m]r\in[m] guesses almost surely (#⁡{i:Ti≠0}≤r\#{\left\{i:T_{i}\neq 0\right\}}\leq r). Let (Bi)i∈[m](B_{i})_{i\in[m]} be independent Bernoulli variables with parameters (bi)i∈[m](b_{i})_{i\in[m]}, independent of all other variables.

  1. 1.

    (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP. If 𝒜\mathcal{A} is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP and bi≤1+e−ε−εDS​(Xi)1+e−εb_{i}\leq\frac{1+e^{-\varepsilon-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DS}}(X_{i})}}{1+e^{-\varepsilon}}, then for any v>0v>0:

    ff-DP. If 𝒜\mathcal{A} is ff-DP and bi≤e−εDS​(Xi)b_{i}\leq e^{-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DS}}(X_{i})}, then for any subset T⊂[r]T\subset[r]:

    ∑k∈Tk​pkm≤f¯​(∑k∈Tr−k+1m​pk−1),\textstyle\sum_{k\in T}\frac{kp_{k}}{m}\leq\bar{f}\bigg(\sum_{k\in T}\frac{r-k+1}{m}p_{k-1}\bigg)\,, (2)

    where pk=ℙ(∑j=1mBj𝟙{Sj=Tj}=k|(Xi)i∈[m])p_{k}\!=\!\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}\!\!B_{j}\mathds{1}_{\left\{S_{j}=T_{j}\right\}}\!=\!k\big|(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right) is the probability of kk correct tampered guesses.

Under (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP, the pointwise tampering parameters bib_{i} are naturally set so that the success probability of the event {Ti′=Si}{\left\{T_{i}^{\prime}=S_{i}\right\}} is eε1+eε\frac{e^{\varepsilon}}{1+e^{\varepsilon}}, by noticing that the probability of this event is bounded by pi​(ε)​bip_{i}(\varepsilon)b_{i}. In the case of ff-DP, bib_{i} can be obtained as the limit when ε→∞\varepsilon\to\infty of the (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP tampering parameters. In both cases, under no distribution shifts we have Bi=1B_{i}=1 almost surely, recovering known One-Run audit results [37, 25]. For (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP, Equation 1 directly bounds the success rate’s right tail of the tampered MIA. In the ff-DP case, the indirect bound (2) can be used to upper-bound the right tail of the success rate, by applying successively Equation 2 to subsets of the form {r′,r′+1,…,r}{\left\{r^{\prime},r^{\prime}+1,\ldots,r\right\}} for r′≤rr^{\prime}\leq r, yielding Algorithm 2. While the proof of Theorem 5.1.1 (Section C.1) draws inspiration from Steinke et al. The error term αr,ε​(v)\alpha_{r,\varepsilon}(v) differs slightly from that of Steinke et al. [37], but is expected to be of same order 𝒪⁡(1/r)\mathcal{O}(1/r) for reasonable parameter values. The proof of Theorem 5.1.2 (Appendix E) is inspired by [25].

While adversary guesses TiT_{i} are obtained by thresholding MIA confidence scores, Theorem 5.1 suggests a natural propensity-aware adversary that further modulates this thresholding via the tampering parameter bib_{i} (see Section 7).

6 Propensity Scores Estimation and Uncertainty Quantification

As defined in Section 3 and applied in Sections 4 and 5, the propensity scores π⁡(Xi)\pi(X_{i}) are critical for isolating distribution shift from true algorithmic privacy leakage. This section clarifies our methodology for estimating them and quantifying their associated uncertainty. First, our algorithms yield valid DP rejections provided that the estimated scores are either exact or pessimistic, as formalized in Corollary 2. The safety requirement for the auditor is thus one-sided: overestimating overlap can invalidate the audit by failing to penalize enough, while underestimating overlap attributes more signal to distribution shift, making the audit strictly more conservative while preserving validity.

Corollary 2.

If min⁡(π^i,1−π^i)≤min⁡(π⁡(Xi),1−π⁡(Xi))\min(\hat{\pi}_{i},1-\hat{\pi}_{i})\leq\min(\pi(X_{i}),1-\pi(X_{i})) for all i∈[m]i\in[m] and if the composition or conditional auditing algorithm returns False for (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP (respectively, for ff-DP), then 𝒜\mathcal{A} is not (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP (respectively, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is not ff-DP) with probability 1−p1-p.

Extracting empirical privacy parameters. Hypothesis testing yields high-confidence empirical privacy lower bounds. Let bμ=Falseb_{\mu}=\textsc{False} denote Algorithm 1 rejecting ℋμ\mathcal{H}_{\mu}: “𝒜\mathcal{A} is μ\mu-GDP”. Because rejecting μ\mu-GDP implies rejecting all μ′≤μ\mu^{\prime}\leq\mu, defining μ^=sup{μ≥0∣bμ=False}\hat{\mu}=\sup{\left\{\mu\geq 0\mid b_{\mu}=\textsc{False}\right\}} guarantees μ⋆≥μ^\mu^{\star}\geq\hat{\mu} with probability at least 1−p1-p, given an audit failure probability pp. A similar search applies to pure ε\varepsilon-DP and monotonic (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP hypotheses via Algorithm 9.

Bootstrapped privacy lower bounds. We consider a separate dataset (Xj′,Sj′)​j∈[m′](X_{j}^{\prime},S_{j}^{\prime}){j\in[m^{\prime}]} used for propensity estimation, distinct from the audit dataset (Xi,Si)​i∈[m](X_{i},S_{i}){i\in[m]}. To quantify the statistical uncertainty on empirical privacy lower bounds due to estimated propensity scores, we bootstrap the final empirical privacy lower bound by resampling this dataset. We consider the empirical privacy lower bound μ^\hat{\mu} (for GDP) as a function of propensity scores (π⁡(Xi))i(\pi(X_{i}))_{i}, all the rest (model θ\theta, MIA guesses TiT_{i}, data points XiX_{i}, and memberships SiS_{i}) being fixed, and proceed as follows for KK bootstrapped propensity scores. For k∈[K]k\in[K]: (1) Bootstrap sample: we draw (Xj′(k),Sj′(k))j∈[m′]({X_{j}^{\prime}}^{(k)},{S_{j}^{\prime}}^{(k)})_{j\in[m^{\prime}]} as a random bootstrap sample from (Xj′,Sj′)j∈[m′](X_{j}^{\prime},S_{j}^{\prime})_{j\in[m^{\prime}]} with replacement; (2) Propensity score training: we train π^i(k)\hat{\pi}_{i}^{(k)} on (Xj′(k),Sj′(k))j∈[m′]({X_{j}^{\prime}}^{(k)},{S_{j}^{\prime}}^{(k)})_{j\in[m^{\prime}]}; (3) Privacy lower bound: we feed (π^(k)​(Xi),Ti,Si)i∈[m](\hat{\pi}^{(k)}(X_{i}),T_{i},S_{i})_{i\in[m]} into the auditing algorithm to extract empirical privacy lower bound μ^(k)\hat{\mu}^{(k)}.

Outputting the p′p^{\prime}-lower quantile μ^\hat{\mu} of (μ^(k))k∈[K](\hat{\mu}^{(k)})_{k\in[K]} yields a robust empirical privacy bound valid with probability 1−p−p′1-p-p^{\prime}, splitting the error budget between the audit (pp) and the bootstrap (p′p^{\prime}). The bootstrap’s formal validity assumes standard, albeit practically unverifiable, regularity conditions—such as Hadamard differentiability [41, Chapter 23]—on the mapping from propensity scores (π⁡(Xi))i(\pi(X_{i}))_{i} to the privacy lower bound. The full procedure is detailed in Algorithm 3 (Section B.1).

7 Experiments

Auditing Setup. We measure empirical privacy leakage via μ\mu-GDP. To manage propensity score uncertainty, we compute empirical lower bounds μ^\hat{\mu} using K=600K=600 bootstrap resamples; 0.950.95 overall confidence is achieved by evenly splitting 0.050.05 error budget between hypothesis testing (p=0.025p=0.025) and bootstrap confidence intervals (p′=0.025p^{\prime}=0.025). Standard One-Run baselines ignore distribution shifts and omit bootstrapping. Evaluating m=10,000m=10,000 points per audit, we determine the optimal active guesses r=‖T‖0r=\|T\|_{0} by sweeping abstentions across {9000,9500,9800,9900,9950,9975}\{9000,9500,9800,9900,9950,9975\}.

Datasets. We evaluate Zero-Run auditing across two complementary scenarios: (1) a synthetic high-dimensional noisy sum mechanism (Appendix F), drawing members (𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1}) and non-members (𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0}) from Gaussian distributions with a tunable correlation parameter to control distribution shift. (2) We demonstrate real-world applicability using the WILDS iWildCam benchmark [26], where inherent geographic and environmental shifts between 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} and 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} introduce natural observational disparities.

Propensity Score Estimation. We compute the propensity scores π^​(Xi)\hat{\pi}(X_{i}) using an L2L_{2}-regularized logistic regression [31] with sigmoid (Platt) calibration. For the iWildCam dataset, we establish a balanced baseline by subsampling the data to equal set sizes (n1=n0n_{1}=n_{0}). Image representations are derived from precomputed ViT-base embeddings [11], subsequently reduced to 50 dimensions via PCA. Figure 2(c) visualizes the resulting π^​(Xi)\hat{\pi}(X_{i}) distributions: the purely IID split yields scores clustered loosely around 0.50.5, whereas the out-of-distribution (OOD) split exhibits a bimodal separation, accurately capturing the underlying structural confounding.

Adversaries. The MIA (Algorithm 5) generates raw guesses Ti∈{−1,0,1}T_{i}\in\{-1,0,1\} using the inner product ⟨Xi,θ⟩\langle X_{i},\theta\rangle as its test statistic for the synthetic white-box adversary, while the iWildCam black-box MIA relies on cross-entropy loss. To optimize our conditional audit (Theorem 5.1), which tampers guesses via independent variables Bi∼Ber​(bi)B_{i}\sim\text{Ber}(b_{i}) to yield Ti′=Bi​TiT^{\prime}_{i}=B_{i}T_{i}, we compare two variants. A propensity-unaware adversary selects its top rr guesses based solely on raw model confidence, while a propensity-aware adversary adjusts its confidence scores using the tampering probabilities bib_{i}, abstaining on structurally distinct examples to prioritize algorithmic signal over distribution shift.

Synthetic Data Results. Figure 2(a) evaluates empirical lower bounds (μ^\hat{\mu}) across distribution shift magnitudes. At the IID baseline (zero shift), both uncorrected One-Run auditing and our conditional Zero-Run framework yield identically valid bounds below the theoretical μtrue=0.66\mu_{\text{true}}=0.66. However, as the shift increases and the distributions diverge, the uncorrected One-Run audit yields invalid bounds. The global compositional correction rapidly loses statistical power due to worst-case penalties, and the adversary that does not take the propensity into account eventually loses auditing power as well. In contrast, our propensity-aware conditional correction effectively deconvolves this confounding signal, with an informative empirical bound that remains relatively flat across shift levels.

Real-World Data Results. Figure 2(b) illustrates our framework on the iWildCam benchmark, showing the μ^(k)\hat{\mu}^{(k)} bootstrap density and the extracted conservative 0.025 quantile (p′=0.025p^{\prime}=0.025). Due to severe natural distribution shifts (Figure 2(c)), the global compositional approach and propensity-unaware adversary incur overly conservative penalties, yielding non-positive bounds (and are thus omitted). Conversely, the propensity-aware conditional correction provides a strong lower bound on true memorization. Despite heavy environmental confounding, the Zero-Run audit extracts a valid privacy lower bound for OOD data (μ^=0.645\hat{\mu}=0.645), closely matching the perfectly IID split bound (μ^=0.652\hat{\mu}=0.652). One-run auditing [25] on IID data achieves a 1.7 lower bound, showing that Zero-Run auditing incurs an ≈1\approx 1 penalty from propensity score estimation and uncertainty quantification.

8 Related Work

Interventional Privacy Auditing. Ding et al. [9], Jagielski et al. [19] introduced privacy auditing methods that rely on repeatedly running the audited algorithm with and without a specific data point. These Multi-Run techniques were later refined to obtain tighter guarantees across various settings [29, 5], see Annamalai et al. [1] for an overview. To reduce the computational cost of rerunning the audited algorithm, Steinke et al. [37] proposed a One-Run auditing method for ε\varepsilon-DP and (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP, later extended to ff-DP by Mahloujifar et al. [25]. While our proof techniques draw on these foundational works, their validity inherently depends on randomized membership assignments controlled by the auditor. This interventional requirement motivates the development of Zero-Run auditing methods that can estimate post hoc privacy leakage from a deployed model.

Observational Privacy Auditing. Kalemaj et al. [22] also audits without randomized insertion, but targets the weaker label-DP, assumes identical member and non-member feature distributions, and cannot correct for general feature-level shifts. More closely related is Panoramia [23], which audits (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP using non-members drawn from a generative model. Panoramia acts as a special case of our composition framework, which we strictly generalize in two ways: we support GDP auditing and employ milder overlap assumptions (Assumption 2) by permitting an approximation error δDS>0\delta_{\mathrm{DS}}>0. When δDS=0\delta_{\mathrm{DS}}=0, this recovers Panoramia’s cc-closeness assumption where c=log⁡((1−η)/η)c=\log((1-\eta)/\eta). Furthermore, rather than learning a full generative model, our approach reduces the correction problem to estimating the propensity score function, i.e., a probabilistic binary classifier.

Causal Inference and Distribution Shift. Even et al. [16] evaluate membership inference attacks under distribution shift using causal principles, primarily by reweighting global attack metrics (e.g., AUC). Unlike causal reweighting approaches [16] or generative approximations [23], we do not attempt to construct non-members that approximately follow the distribution of members. Instead, we capture marginal distribution-shift leakage conditional on observations, which does not require a global overlap assumption to be valid. Our audit only requires that Assumption 1 hold, and implicitly relies on local overlaps between members and non-members rather than a global one. As explicited in Proposition 3, valid Zero-Run auditing is impossible without any local overlap (disjoint support).

9 Limitations & Conclusion

Propensity Estimation Limitation. Our zero-run framework relies on being able to properly estimate the propensity score. For natural, high-dimensional data, even under an IID assumption, this is challenging due to finite-sample estimation error, as illustrated in Figure 2(c): although the oracle propensity score is 0.50.5, the estimated scores deviate from this value and induces additional penalization. Finding better, more reliable ways to estimate propensity scores, although orthogonal to our work, will directly benefit our framework and the tightness of our audits.

One-Run & MIA Limitation. While our framework successfully enables post-hoc privacy evaluation, it naturally inherits the limitations of existing One-Run algorithms. First, as observed by the baseline gap in Figure 2, Zero-Run auditing is limited by the finite-sample inefficiency intrinsic to all One-Run methods, meaning empirical bounds will inherently sit somewhat below the theoretical limit [37, 25]. Again, any improvement in this line of work would directly benefit our framework. Second, an audit’s success is deeply tied to the baseline strength of the underlying MIA. In heavily restricted black-box deployments, particularly against DP models [29], relying purely on loss-based attacks, the raw attack signal is often too weak to extract meaningful bounds, independent of our shift corrections.

Auditing and falsifiability of propensity score models. Our observational audit relies on estimated bounds for the propensity scores. Although these bounds cannot be formally certified, they can be empirically falsified: one can treat them as a hypothesis and audit them using Theorem C.1, analogously to a DP claim, rejecting the propensity model when the observed evidence contradicts the claimed bounds. This test is necessarily one-sided: passing it does not prove the bounds correct, but only indicates that no violation was found with the available data and auditing power. This motivates releasing the propensity score bounds, audit dataset, and auditing procedure together with the final audit result. A skeptic can then challenge the claimed correction for distribution shift by constructing a stronger MIA that exploits the shift beyond what the released bounds allow. Thus, while the propensity model remains unverifiable in a formal sense, openness and adversarial testing make the audit computationally falsifiable and more trustworthy in practice.

The main lesson is that post-hoc privacy auditing is possible, but only as an observational inference problem. Distribution shift cannot be ignored: it is itself a source of membership information. Propensity scores provide the right language for quantifying this source, and our results show how to convert propensity bounds into valid empirical lower bounds on algorithmic privacy leakage.

A.3 The Central Role of Propensity Scores in Privacy Auditing with Distribution Shift

Next results motivate the role of π\pi in our analysis by showing that when ℙ1≠ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{1}\neq\mathbb{P}_{0}, the classical inequality relating true positive and true negative rates (TPR and FPR) for a MIA on an ff-DP algorithm is altered, as shown by the following result. The proof is particularly instructive due to its simplicity, illustrating how propensity scores naturally arise when auditing under distribution shift.

Proposition 1.

Assume that Assumption 1 holds and that (Xi,Si,Ti)i∈[m](X_{i},S_{i},T_{i})_{i\in[m]} are independent. Then,

𝔼⁡[Aiπ⁡(Xi)​ℙ​(Ti=1|Si=1,Xi)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{A_{i}}{\pi(X_{i})}\mathbb{P}\left(T_{i}=1|S_{i}=1,X_{i}\right)\right] (4)
≤f¯​(𝔼⁡[1−Ai1−π⁡(Xi)​ℙ​(Ti=1|Si=−1,Xi)]),\displaystyle\leq\bar{f}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1-A_{i}}{1-\pi(X_{i})}\mathbb{P}\left(T_{i}=1|S_{i}=-1,X_{i}\right)\right]\right)\,,

where Ai=𝟙{Si=1}=Si+12A_{i}=\mathds{1}_{\left\{S_{i}=1\right\}}=\frac{S_{i}+1}{2}.

Proof of Proposition 1.

by definition of f−f-DP. Now, let’s take the average over (S¯(−i),X¯(−i))(\bar{S}^{(-i)},\bar{X}^{(-i)}) and use the independence assumption made in Proposition 1:

𝔼S¯(−i),X¯(−i)​ℙ​(Ti=1|Si=1,S¯(−i),X¯)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bar{S}^{(-i)},\bar{X}^{(-i)}}\mathbb{P}\left(T_{i}=1|S_{i}=1,\bar{S}^{(-i)},\bar{X}\right)

by concavity of f¯\bar{f}, leading to:

A.6 Impossibility Result

A pp-valid audit algorithm for the privacy hypothesis ’ff-DP’ is abstracted as a mapping:

ℬf:(𝒟0,𝒟1,θ)∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)×𝒫⁡(𝒳)×Θ↦b∈{True,False},\mathcal{B}_{f}:(\mathcal{D}_{0},\mathcal{D}_{1},\theta)\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})\times\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})\times\Theta\mapsto b\in{\left\{\textsc{True},\textsc{False}\right\}}\,,

which satisfies, for any ff-DP algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A}, for any 𝒟train∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}), any 𝒟1⊂𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{1}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} and 𝒟0⊂𝒳∖𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{0}\subset\mathcal{X}\setminus\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}:

ℙ⁡(ℬf​(𝒟0,𝒟1,𝒜⁡(𝒟))=False)≤p.\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{B}_{f}(\mathcal{D}_{0},\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}))=\textsc{False}\right)\leq p\,.

In other words, ℬf\mathcal{B}_{f} confidently rejects the privacy hypothesis with probability 1−p1-p, if False is outputted.

Next proposition shows that if the overlap assumption is no satisfied, no pp-valid audit algorithm can make meaningful audits.

Proposition 3 (Impossibility).

There exists two distributions ℙ1,ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{1},\mathbb{P}_{0} and an algorithm 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime} which does not satisfy ε′\varepsilon^{\prime}-DP for any ε′>0\varepsilon^{\prime}>0, and such that if 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} and 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} are respectively samples drawn from ℙ1\mathbb{P}_{1} and ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{0}, any pp-valid audit algorithm for any ε\varepsilon-DP hypothesis yields:

ℙ⁡(ℬε​(𝒟0,𝒟1,𝒜′​(𝒟1))=False)≤p.\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}(\mathcal{D}_{0},\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{A}^{\prime}(\mathcal{D}_{1}))=\textsc{False}\right)\leq p\,.

In other words, no audit algorithm can reject confidently any privacy level ε\varepsilon, despite 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime} not satisfying any ε′\varepsilon^{\prime}-DP..

Proof.

To simplify, assume that 𝒳=ℝ\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}. Let 𝒳=𝒳0∪𝒳1\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_{0}\cup\mathcal{X}_{1} with 𝒳0∩𝒳1=∅\mathcal{X}_{0}\cap\mathcal{X}_{1}=\emptyset, and ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{0} and ℙ1\mathbb{P}_{1} be distributions having respective supports 𝒳0\mathcal{X}_{0} and 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1}. Let 𝒜⁡(𝒟)\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}) be the algorithm defined as, for any dataset 𝒟⊂𝒳\mathcal{D}\subset\mathcal{X}:

𝒜(𝒟):x∈𝒳↦𝟙{x∈𝒳1}.\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}):x\in\mathcal{X}\mapsto\mathds{1}_{\left\{x\in\mathcal{X}_{1}\right\}}\,.

𝒜\mathcal{A} is 00-DP since it is deterministic and does not depend on the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Let then 𝒜′​(𝒟)\mathcal{A}^{\prime}(\mathcal{D}) be the algorithm defined as, for any datset 𝒟⊂𝒳\mathcal{D}\subset\mathcal{X}:

𝒜′(𝒟):x∈𝒳↦𝟙{x∈𝒳1 or x∈𝒟}.\mathcal{A}^{\prime}(\mathcal{D}):x\in\mathcal{X}\mapsto\mathds{1}_{\left\{x\in\mathcal{X}_{1}\text{ or }x\in\mathcal{D}\right\}}\,.

𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime} is not ε\varepsilon-DP for any ε′>0\varepsilon^{\prime}>0 (take 𝒟={x}\mathcal{D}={\left\{x\right\}} with x∈𝒳1x\in\mathcal{X}_{1} and x∈𝒳0x\in\mathcal{X}_{0}). However, for 𝒟1⊂𝒳1\mathcal{D}_{1}\subset\mathcal{X}_{1}, we always have that 𝒜⁡(𝒟1)=𝒜⁡(𝒟1′)\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}_{1})=\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{1}). Thus,

ℙ⁡(ℬε​(𝒟0,𝒟1,𝒜′​(𝒟1))=False)=ℙ⁡(ℬε​(𝒟0,𝒟1,𝒜⁡(𝒟1))=False)≤p,\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}(\mathcal{D}_{0},\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{A}^{\prime}(\mathcal{D}_{1}))=\textsc{False}\right)=\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}(\mathcal{D}_{0},\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}_{1}))=\textsc{False}\right)\leq p\,,

for any pp-valid audit algorithm ℬε\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon} for the ε\varepsilon-DP privacy hypothesis.

∎

Appendix B Privacy Auditing Algorithms

B.1 Bootstrap Algorithm

Algorithm 3 formalizes our bootstrap precedure. Given a function Ψ:[0,1]m→ℝ\Psi:[0,1]^{m}\to\mathbb{R}, the bootstrap procedure yields confidence intervals around:

Ψ⁡((π⁡(Xi))i∈[m]),\Psi((\pi(X_{i}))_{i\in[m]})\,,

using only estimates of the propensity scores. We then use this by seeing empirical lower bounds as functions of the propensity scores, all the rest being fixed.

B.2 Propensity scores learning algorithm with crossfitting

When we do not have enough samples, instead of learning the propensity score on a held-out dataset as we describe in Section 6, cross-fitting can be used as follows to avoid overfitting. Bootstrap can then be done on each half of the dataset when learning the propensity score.

B.3 Memberhsip Inference Attack Algorithm

Algorithm 5 describes how a MIA is performed: a confidence score Yi∈ℝY_{i}\in\mathbb{R} is first computed for every datapoint. The larger YiY_{i}, the more confident the attacker is about XiX_{i} begin a member (i.e., Si=1S_{i}=1). Guesses gig_{i} are then made using these scores for all datapoints. For instance, a threshold tt can be computed, and the guess can be set as gi=𝟙{Yi≥t}−𝟙{Yi<t}g_{i}=\mathds{1}_{\left\{Y_{i}\geq t\right\}}-\mathds{1}_{\left\{Y_{i}<t\right\}}. In order to keep datapoints for which we are most confident about their membership or non-memberhsip, an abstention step is finally performed, by setting low-confidence guesses to 0, thereby obtaining a vector of guesses and abstentions T∈{−1,0,1}T\in{\left\{-1,0,1\right\}}.

B.4 (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP Auditing Algorithm (under worst-case distribution shift bounds)

We use Corollary 1 and Steinke et al. [37]’s audit algorithm for (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP. To simplify the algorithm, we assume that the MIA outputs guesses (Ti)i∈[m](T_{i})_{i\in[m]} which satisfy ‖T‖0=r{{\left\|T\right\|}}_{0}=r almost surely, for some fixed r∈[m]r\in[m]. This can be ensured by simply maximizing ∑iYi​Ti\sum_{i}Y_{i}T_{i} over T∈{−1,0,1}mT\in{\left\{-1,0,1\right\}}^{m} verifying {Ti=±1}=k±{\left\{T_{i}=\pm 1\right\}}=k_{\pm}, for k++k−=rk_{+}+k_{-}=r. Algorithm 6 instantiates Steinke et al. [37]’s audit algorithm under this assumption. Proposition 4 then follows from Steinke et al. [37, Corollary 5.4].

Proposition 4.

Let ε,δ>0\varepsilon,\delta>0. Assume that 1 and 2 hold and that ‖T‖0=r{{\left\|T\right\|}}_{0}=r almost surely. Then, Algorithm 6 is pp-valid: if Algorithm 6 outputs False, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is not (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP with probability 1−p1-p.

B.5 μ\mu-GDP Auditing Algorithm (under worst-case distribution shift bounds)

We use Corollary 1 and Mahloujifar et al. [25]’s audit algorithm for general ff-DP. We assume that the MIA outputs guesses (Ti)i∈[m](T_{i})_{i\in[m]} which satisfy ‖T‖0=r{{\left\|T\right\|}}_{0}=r almost surely, for some fixed r∈[m]r\in[m]. This can be ensured by simply maximizing ∑iYi​Ti\sum_{i}Y_{i}T_{i} over T∈{−1,0,1}mT\in{\left\{-1,0,1\right\}}^{m} verifying {Ti=±1}=k±{\left\{T_{i}=\pm 1\right\}}=k_{\pm}, for k++k−=rk_{+}+k_{-}=r. Algorithm 6 instantiates Mahloujifar et al. [25]’s audit algorithm under this assumption, for the tradeoff function G′=Gμ2+μDS2⊗fδDSG^{\prime}=G_{\sqrt{\mu^{2}+\mu_{\mathrm{DS}}^{2}}}\otimes f_{\delta_{\mathrm{DS}}}, which writes as:

G′(p)={(1−δDS)​Gμ2+μDS2​(p1−δDS)if0≤p≤1−δDS,0else.G^{\prime}(p)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &(1-\delta_{\mathrm{DS}})G_{\sqrt{\mu^{2}+\mu_{\mathrm{DS}}^{2}}}(\tfrac{p}{1-\delta_{\mathrm{DS}}})\quad\text{if}\quad 0\leq p\leq 1-\delta_{\mathrm{DS}}\,,\\ &0\qquad\text{else.}\end{aligned}\right. (5)

Proposition 5 then follows from Mahloujifar et al. [25, Theorem 10].

Proposition 5.

Let μ>0\mu>0. Assume that 1 and 2 hold and that ‖T‖0=r{{\left\|T\right\|}}_{0}=r almost surely. Then, Algorithm 7 is pp-valid: if Algorithm 7 outputs False, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is not μ\mu-GDP with probability 1−p1-p.

The error probability δDS\delta_{\mathrm{DS}} can also be put in the error probability of the audit, allowing us to use Mahloujifar et al. [25]’s auditing algorithm for the GDP tradeoff function, yielding a (p+δDS)(p+\delta_{\mathrm{DS}})-valid audit (instead pf pp-valid). This is what we describe in the discussion after Corollary 1, and what next algorithm and corollary formalize.

Proposition 6.

Let μ>0\mu>0. Assume that 1 and 2 hold and that ‖T‖0=r{{\left\|T\right\|}}_{0}=r almost surely. Then, Algorithm 7 is (p+δDS)(p+\delta_{\mathrm{DS}})-valid: if Algorithm 8 outputs False, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is not μ\mu-GDP with probability 1−p−δDS1-p-\delta_{\mathrm{DS}}.

Appendix C Conditional (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-Auditing

C.1 Conditional ε\varepsilon-DP Auditing

We now present a relaxed version of Theorem 5.1.1 with δ=0\delta=0. We include this simplified result for its proof simplicity and clarity of exposure, as well as for its use for rejecting propensity score models, as explained in next paragraph.

Rejecting propensity score models. Theorem C.1 can additionally be used to audit a propensity score model: setting ε=0\varepsilon=0 and bib_{i} obtained using a propensity score model π^\hat{\pi}, having a large success rate for the obtained tampered MIA which only hinges on distribution shift means that π^\hat{\pi} does not not penalize enough distribution shifts, yielding a natural hypothesis test.

C.2 Proof of Theorem 5.1.1

We now proceed to the proof of Theorem 5.1.1, starting with the following intermediate result.

C.3 Conditional Zero-Run (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP Auditing Algorithm

Appendix D Conditional Approximate DP Auditing Without Tampering

In this section, we show that approximate DP can be audited in Zero-Run, without tampering. In order to do so, instead of multiplying MIA guesses by independent Bernoulli variables in order to tamper with their confidence, we adapt the success rate, which need to take into account MIA overconfidence. While in the pure DP setting, both results would yield equivalent results, in the approximate DP case the tampering results are stronger, as they yield milder δ\delta dependence. However, the obtained MIA success rate bounds here are conditioned also on TiT_{i}.

Proposition 8.

≤δ′.\displaystyle\leq\delta^{\prime}\,.

Each element in the sum defining BmB_{m} is of bounded first moment of order δ′\delta^{\prime}, but the two difficulties are that: these events are not independent, and these events are not independent of random variables TiT_{i}, enabling us to only be able to use a basic Markov inequality. We thus have, on the one hand:

𝔼⁡[Bm|X¯]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[B_{m}|\bar{X}\right] ≤m​δ′.\displaystyle\leq m\delta^{\prime}\,.

Using Markov inequality,

ℙ⁡(Bm>v|X¯)≤m​δ′v,\mathbb{P}\left(B_{m}>v|\bar{X}\right)\leq\frac{m\delta^{\prime}}{v}\,,

and thus, for any u,v>0u,v>0:

ℙ⁡(∑i=1mmax⁡(0,Si​Ti)>u|X¯,T¯)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\max(0,S_{i}T_{i})>u|\bar{X},\bar{T}\right)
≤ℙ⁡(Am>u−Bm|X¯,T¯)\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left(A_{m}>u-B_{m}|\bar{X},\bar{T}\right)
≤ℙ(∑i=1m|Ti|ξi>u−v,Bm≤v|X¯,T¯)+ℙ(∑i=1m|Ti|ξi>u−Bm,Bm≥v|X¯,T¯)\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}|T_{i}|\xi_{i}>u-v,B_{m}\leq v|\bar{X},\bar{T}\right)+\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}|T_{i}|\xi_{i}>u-B_{m},B_{m}\geq v|\bar{X},\bar{T}\right)
≤ℙ⁡(∑i=1m|Ti|​ξi>u−v|X¯,T¯)+ℙ⁡(Bm≥v|X¯,T¯).\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}|T_{i}|\xi_{i}>u-v|\bar{X},\bar{T}\right)+\mathbb{P}\left(B_{m}\geq v|\bar{X},\bar{T}\right)\,.

Then, since using Markov inequality:

𝔼⁡[ℙ⁡(Bm≥v|X¯,T¯)|X¯]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{P}\left(B_{m}\geq v|\bar{X},\bar{T}\right)|\bar{X}\right]
=ℙ⁡(Bm≥v|X¯)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(B_{m}\geq v|\bar{X}\right)
≤m​δ′v,\displaystyle\leq\frac{m\delta^{\prime}}{v}\,,

using yet again Markov inequality, for any v,w>0v,w>0:

ℙ⁡(ℙ⁡(Bm≥v|X¯,T¯)>w)≤2​m​δ′v​w,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{P}\left(B_{m}\geq v|\bar{X},\bar{T}\right)>w\right)\leq\frac{2m\delta^{\prime}}{vw}\,,

and we conclude by taking w=(m​δ′v)1/2w=\left(\frac{m\delta^{\prime}}{v}\right)^{1/2}. ∎

D.4 Proof of Theorem D.2

Proof of Theorem D.2.

The proof follows by combining Proposition 7 with Theorem D.3. ∎

We now prove Theorem 5.1.2. Although the remaining arguments are exactly the same as in Mahloujifar et al. [25], we include them for completeness.

Proof of Theorem 5.1.2.

We first state the following lemma [25, Proposition 12].

Lemma 2.

f′f^{\prime} is increasing and concave.

Proof of Lemma 2.

For t<t′t<t^{\prime}, we have that for all α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} such that t−αt-\alpha and t′−αt^{\prime}-\alpha are in [0,1][0,1]:

α+f⁡(t−α)≥α+f⁡(t−α),\alpha+f(t-\alpha)\geq\alpha+f(t-\alpha)\,,

since ff is decreasing. Thus, f⁡(t)≤f⁡(t′)f(t)\leq f(t^{\prime}) and ff is increasing.

For concavity, let t,t′∈ℝt,t^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}. By convexity of ff, for any α,α′∈ℝ\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R} such that t−αt-\alpha and t′−α′t^{\prime}-\alpha^{\prime} are in [0,1][0,1]:

f⁡(t+t′2−α+α′2)≤f⁡(t−α)+f⁡(t′−α′)2,f(\frac{t+t^{\prime}}{2}-\frac{\alpha+\alpha^{\prime}}{2})\leq\frac{f(t-\alpha)+f(t^{\prime}-\alpha^{\prime})}{2}\,,

by convexity of ff. Thus, if α,α′\alpha,\alpha^{\prime} satisfy f⁡(t−α)+α≤1f(t-\alpha)+\alpha\leq 1 and f⁡(t′−α′)+α′≤1f(t^{\prime}-\alpha^{\prime})+\alpha^{\prime}\leq 1, we have

α+α′2+α+f⁡(t−α)+α′+f⁡(t′−α)2≤1,\frac{\alpha+\alpha^{\prime}}{2}+\frac{\alpha+f(t-\alpha)+\alpha^{\prime}+f(t^{\prime}-\alpha)}{2}\leq 1\,,

and thus α+α′2+f⁡(t+t′2−α+α′2)≤1\frac{\alpha+\alpha^{\prime}}{2}+f(\frac{t+t^{\prime}}{2}-\frac{\alpha+\alpha^{\prime}}{2})\leq 1. We can thus conclude that f⁡(t+t′2)≥α+α′2f(\frac{t+t^{\prime}}{2})\geq\frac{\alpha+\alpha^{\prime}}{2} and taking the sup over α,α′\alpha,\alpha^{\prime} satisfying f⁡(t−α)+α≤1f(t-\alpha)+\alpha\leq 1 and f⁡(t′−α′)+α′≤1f(t^{\prime}-\alpha^{\prime})+\alpha^{\prime}\leq 1, we have concavity. ∎

As in Mahloujifar et al. [25, Theorem 9], we assume that the adversary makes guesses on all mm inputs with a vector q∈{0,1}mq\in{\left\{0,1\right\}}^{m} with exactly rr 1’s and m−rm-r 0’s. Only correct guesses that are in locations where qi=1q_{i}=1 are counted. If ti=𝟙{Si=Ti′}t_{i}=\mathds{1}_{\left\{S_{i}=T_{i}^{\prime}\right\}}, we thus have

pk\displaystyle p_{k} =ℙ⁡(∑i=1mti​qi=k|(Xi)i∈[m])\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}t_{i}q_{i}=k\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)
=ℙ⁡(∑i=2mti​qi=k−1​ and ​t1=1​ and ​q1=1|(Xi)i∈[m])\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{i}q_{i}=k-1\text{ and }t_{1}=1\text{ and }q_{1}=1\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)
+ℙ⁡(∑i=2mti​qi=k​ and ​t1​q1=0|(Xi)i∈[m]).\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{i}q_{i}=k\text{ and }t_{1}q_{1}=0\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)\,.

Here, we could use Lemma 1, which would yield:

ℙ⁡(∑i=2mti​qi=k−1​ and ​t1=1​ and ​q1=1|(Xi)i∈[m])\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{i}q_{i}=k-1\text{ and }t_{1}=1\text{ and }q_{1}=1\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)
≤f′​(ℙ⁡(∑i=2mti​qi=k−1​ and ​q1=1|(Xi)i∈[m])).\displaystyle\leq f^{\prime}\left(\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{i}q_{i}=k-1\text{ and }q_{1}=1\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)\right)\,.

To obtain sharper bounds, we instead sum over all k∈Tk\in T and use the same reasoning:

∑k∈Tpk\displaystyle\sum_{k\in T}p_{k} =∑k∈Tℙ⁡(∑i=1mti​qi=k|(Xi)i∈[m])\displaystyle=\sum_{k\in T}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}t_{i}q_{i}=k\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)
=∑k∈Tℙ⁡(∑i=2mti​qi=k−1​ and ​t1=1​ and ​q1=1|(Xi)i∈[m])\displaystyle=\sum_{k\in T}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{i}q_{i}=k-1\text{ and }t_{1}=1\text{ and }q_{1}=1\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)
+ℙ⁡(∑i=2mti​qi=k​ and ​t1​q1=0|(Xi)i∈[m])\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{i}q_{i}=k\text{ and }t_{1}q_{1}=0\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)
=ℙ⁡(1+∑i=2mti​qi∈T​ and ​t1=1​ and ​q1=1|(Xi)i∈[m])\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(1+\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{i}q_{i}\in T\text{ and }t_{1}=1\text{ and }q_{1}=1\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)
+ℙ⁡(∑i=2mti​qi∈T​ and ​t1​q1=0|(Xi)i∈[m]).\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{i}q_{i}\in T\text{ and }t_{1}q_{1}=0\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)\,.

We now use Lemma 1 on the first term:

∑k∈Tpk\displaystyle\sum_{k\in T}p_{k} ≤f′​(ℙ⁡(1+∑i=2mti​qi∈T​ and ​q1=1|(Xi)i∈[m]))\displaystyle\leq f^{\prime}\left(\mathbb{P}\left(1+\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{i}q_{i}\in T\text{ and }q_{1}=1\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)\right)
+ℙ⁡(∑i=2mti​qi∈T​ and ​t1​q1=0|(Xi)i∈[m]).\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{i}q_{i}\in T\text{ and }t_{1}q_{1}=0\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)\,.

The RHS of the bound is now invariant under a permutation of the order of indices, so that for a random permutation π\pi sampled uniformly at random in all permutations on [n][n], we have:

∑k∈Tpk\displaystyle\sum_{k\in T}p_{k} ≤𝔼π​f′​(ℙ⁡(1+∑i=2mtπ⁡(i)​qπ⁡(i)∈T​ and ​qπ⁡(1)=1|(Xi)i∈[m]))\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\pi}f^{\prime}\left(\mathbb{P}\left(1+\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{\pi(i)}q_{\pi(i)}\in T\text{ and }q_{\pi(1)}=1\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)\right)
+𝔼π​ℙ​(∑i=2mtπ⁡(i)​qπ⁡(i)∈T​ and ​tπ⁡(1)​qπ⁡(1)=0|(Xi)i∈[m])\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{\pi(i)}q_{\pi(i)}\in T\text{ and }t_{\pi(1)}q_{\pi(1)}=0\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)
≤f′​(𝔼π​ℙ​(1+∑i=2mtπ⁡(i)​qπ⁡(i)∈T​ and ​qπ⁡(1)=1|(Xi)i∈[m]))\displaystyle\leq f^{\prime}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\mathbb{P}\left(1+\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{\pi(i)}q_{\pi(i)}\in T\text{ and }q_{\pi(1)}=1\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)\right)
+𝔼π​ℙ​(∑i=2mtπ⁡(i)​qπ⁡(i)∈T​ and ​tπ⁡(1)​qπ⁡(1)=0|(Xi)i∈[m]),\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{\pi(i)}q_{\pi(i)}\in T\text{ and }t_{\pi(1)}q_{\pi(1)}=0\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)\,,

using concavity of f′f^{\prime}. The reasoning is then the same as Mahloujifar et al. [25]: when permuting the order, ∑i=2mtπ⁡(i)​qπ⁡(i)=k\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{\pi(i)}q_{\pi(i)}=k and tπ⁡(1)​qπ⁡(1)=0t_{\pi(1)}q_{\pi(1)}=0 count each instances t​qtq with exactly kk non-zero locations, for (m−k)×(m−1)!(m-k)\times(m-1)! times, leading to:

𝔼π​ℙ​(∑i=2mtπ⁡(i)​qπ⁡(i)∈T​ and ​tπ⁡(1)​qπ⁡(1)=0|(Xi)i∈[m])=∑k∈Tm−km​pk.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{\pi(i)}q_{\pi(i)}\in T\text{ and }t_{\pi(1)}q_{\pi(1)}=0\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)=\sum_{k\in T}\frac{m-k}{m}p_{k}\,.

Similarly for the other term, ∑i=2mtπ⁡(i)​qπ⁡(i)=k−1\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{\pi(i)}q_{\pi(i)}=k-1 and qπ⁡(1)=1q_{\pi(1)}=1 count each instances t,qt,q that satisfy ti​qi=1t_{i}q_{i}=1 for k−1k-1 indices exactly ((r−k+1)​(m−1)!(r-k+1)(m-1)! times each) and each instances t,qt,q that satisfy ti​qi=1t_{i}q_{i}=1 for kk indices exactly (k⁡(m−1)!k(m-1)! times each), leading to:

𝔼π​ℙ​(1+∑i=2mtπ⁡(i)​qπ⁡(i)∈T​ and ​qπ⁡(1)=1|(Xi)i∈[m])=∑k∈Tkm​pk+r−k+1m​pk−1.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\mathbb{P}\left(1+\sum_{i=2}^{m}t_{\pi(i)}q_{\pi(i)}\in T\text{ and }q_{\pi(1)}=1\,\big|\,(X_{i})_{i\in[m]}\right)=\sum_{k\in T}\frac{k}{m}p_{k}+\frac{r-k+1}{m}p_{k-1}\,.

leading to:

=f¯​(∑k∈Tr−k+1m​pk−1),\displaystyle=\bar{f}\left(\sum_{k\in T}\frac{r-k+1}{m}p_{k-1}\right)\,,

since f¯=1−f\bar{f}=1-f and ff is decreasing. This concludes the proof. ∎

Appendix F Experimental Synthetic Distribution Shift

To rigorously evaluate the deconvolution of privacy leakage from dataset shift, we construct a high-dimensional synthetic Membership Inference Attack (MIA) environment. The procedure isolates empirical privacy leakage by controlling both the algorithmic signal-to-noise ratio and the underlying structural dataset shift.

Let NN be the total dataset size, partitioned equally into a member set 𝒟mem\mathcal{D}_{\text{mem}} and a non-member set 𝒟non\mathcal{D}_{\text{non}}, and let dd be the feature dimensionality. We first sample a fixed global direction vector 𝝁∈ℝd\bm{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:

𝒗∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰d),𝝁=𝒗‖𝒗‖2\bm{v}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}_{d}),\quad\bm{\mu}=\frac{\bm{v}}{\|\bm{v}\|_{2}} (8)

To strictly enforce a bounded L2L_{2} sensitivity for the downstream differential privacy mechanism, we define a generative function g⁡(γ)g(\gamma) that draws a feature vector shifted along 𝝁\bm{\mu} with bias strength γ\gamma, and subsequently projects it onto the unit hypersphere:

𝒙~∼𝒩⁡(γ​𝝁,𝑰d),𝒙=𝒙~‖𝒙~‖2\bm{\tilde{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\gamma\bm{\mu},\bm{I}_{d}),\quad\bm{x}=\frac{\bm{\tilde{x}}}{\|\bm{\tilde{x}}\|_{2}} (9)

This projection step ensures that every single data record inherently satisfies ‖𝒙‖2=1\|\bm{x}\|_{2}=1. We construct the target model’s training set by generating members with a strong baseline bias γbase\gamma_{\text{base}}:

∀𝒙∈𝒟mem,𝒙∼g⁡(γbase)\forall\bm{x}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{mem}},\quad\bm{x}\sim g(\gamma_{\text{base}}) (10)

For the non-members, we modulate the bias strength to simulate evaluation environments with and without structural shift, parameterized by an alignment decay ratio ρ∈(0,1]\rho\in(0,1]:

  • •

    IID Setting (No Shift): The non-members are identically distributed to the members using γnon=γbase\gamma_{\text{non}}=\gamma_{\text{base}}.

  • •

    OOD Setting (Dataset Shift): The non-members are drawn using an attenuated bias strength γnon=ρ⋅γbase\gamma_{\text{non}}=\rho\cdot\gamma_{\text{base}}. Because the shift attenuates the signal purely along the axis of the base vector 𝝁\bm{\mu}, it creates a structural dataset gap strictly aligned with the adversary’s target objective.

We abstract the training of the machine learning model by computing a differentially private sum of the members’ feature vectors. Under the standard add/remove adjacency definition, the global L2L_{2} sensitivity of the sum query is strictly bounded by the maximum norm of a single vector:

Δ2=max𝒙⁡‖𝒙‖2=1\Delta_{2}=\max_{\bm{x}}\|\bm{x}\|_{2}=1 (11)

We apply the Gaussian mechanism by adding isotropic Gaussian noise calibrated to a scale σ>0\sigma>0:

𝜽priv=∑𝒙∈𝒟mem𝒙+𝜼,where ​𝜼∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,σ2​𝑰d)\bm{\theta}_{\text{priv}}=\sum_{\bm{x}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{mem}}}\bm{x}+\bm{\eta},\quad\text{where }\bm{\eta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{d}) (12)

Releasing 𝜽priv\bm{\theta}_{\text{priv}} rigorously guarantees μ\mu-Gaussian Differential Privacy (μ\mu-GDP) with a true algorithmic privacy limit bounded at μtrue=Δ2/σ=1/σ\mu_{\text{true}}=\Delta_{2}/\sigma=1/\sigma.

The adversary attempts to distinguish members from non-members via white-box access to the target model. The attacker computes a linear test statistic against the public DP-released vector for all queried samples 𝒙∈𝒟mem∪𝒟non\bm{x}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{mem}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\text{non}}:

sMIA​(𝒙)=⟨𝒙,𝜽priv⟩s_{\text{MIA}}(\bm{x})=\langle\bm{x},\bm{\theta}_{\text{priv}}\rangle (13)

Because the structural dataset shift between members and non-members occurs along the same vector 𝝁\bm{\mu} as the principal component of 𝜽priv\bm{\theta}_{\text{priv}}, the shift systematically inflates the attacker’s observed signal (μtot\mu_{\text{tot}}) independently of any true algorithmic memorization.

To explicitly isolate the true empirical leakage from the confounding dataset shift, the auditor computes propensity scores π^i≈P⁡(yi=1∣𝒙i)\hat{\pi}_{i}\approx P(y_{i}=1\mid\bm{x}_{i}) using an L2L_{2}-regularized Logistic Regression across the standardized feature space. These propensity scores quantify the structural ceiling of the dataset shift (μds\mu_{\text{ds}}), allowing the auditor to cleanly deconvolve the overall observed attack strength (μtot\mu_{\text{tot}}) back into the true, Zero-Run algorithmic leakage:

μleak=max⁡(0,μtot2−μds2)\mu_{\text{leak}}=\sqrt{\max\left(0,\,\mu_{\text{tot}}^{2}-\mu_{\text{ds}}^{2}\right)} (14)
